extracted.intended_audience: general readers, policymakers, and nuclear safety professionals interested in lessons from the Fukushima Daiichi accident
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted standards, design changes, and preparedness criteria discussed in the Fukushima Daiichi accident article — practical and regulatory lessons for nuclear reactor safety, emergency preparedness, and post-accident response. Focuses on reactor design, venting/filtration, backup power/hardening, regulation, and emergency planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of hydrogen control devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Had such devices been positioned at the top of the reactor buildings, where hydrogen gas collected, the explosions would not have occurred and the releases of radioactive isotopes may have been less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Install hydrogen mitigation devices (e.g., recombiners, hydrogen venting controls) at locations where hydrogen accumulates (top of reactor buildings) to prevent explosions and limit radioactive releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Filtered Containment Venting Systems (FCVS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unpowered filtering systems on containment building vent lines, known as Filtered Containment Venting Systems (FCVS), can safely catch radioactive materials and thereby allow reactor core depressurization, with steam and hydrogen venting with minimal radioactivity emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit containment vent lines with FCVS to enable depressurization while minimizing release of radioactive materials; unpowered/passive designs are highlighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: External water-tank filtration systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Filtration using an external water tank system is the most common established system in European countries, with the water tank positioned outside the containment building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement external water-tank based filtration located outside containment as an established method to capture radionuclides during venting; consider proven regional practices when retrofitting older plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backup battery supply for flood/tsunami-prone Generation II reactors
rubrics_metrics.description: For Generation II reactors located in flood or tsunami prone areas, a 3+ day supply of back-up batteries has become an informal industry standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide at least three days (preferably more) of independent battery power for critical instrumentation/controls in reactors exposed to prolonged loss-of-offsite power scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardening of backup diesel generator rooms
rubrics_metrics.description: Another change is to harden the location of back-up diesel generator rooms with water-tight, blast-resistant doors and heat sinks, similar to those used by nuclear submarines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and retrofit generator rooms to be watertight and blast-resistant, include thermal management (heat sinks), and physically protect EDGs from flooding, tsunami, and explosion effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of passive nuclear safety features in Generation III designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many constructed Generation III reactors adopt the principle of passive nuclear safety. They take advantage of convection and gravity to ensure an adequate supply of cooling water to handle the decay heat, without the use of pumps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer passive safety systems (gravity- and convection-driven cooling) that do not rely on active pumps or external power to remove decay heat following an event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robotics for severe-radiation disaster response must be dexterous and robust
rubrics_metrics.description: The accident illustrated that robots lacked sufficient dexterity and robustness to perform critical tasks. In response to this shortcoming, a series of competitions were hosted by DARPA to accelerate the development of humanoid robots that could supplement relief efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and procure disaster-response robots with demonstrated dexterity, robustness, and radiation tolerance; test under realistic high-radiation and degraded-environment conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic organizational safety requirements (risk assessment, containment planning, evacuation plans)
rubrics_metrics.description: The NAIIC found that the causes of the accident had been foreseeable, and that TEPCO had failed to meet basic safety requirements such as risk assessment, preparing for containing collateral damage, and developing evacuation plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain up-to-date, comprehensive risk assessments; prepare plans for containment of collateral damage; and develop, rehearse, and communicate evacuation plans to reduce harm in foreseeable accident scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid regulatory conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: IAEA faulted lax oversight by the Japanese Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, saying the ministry faced an inherent conflict of interest as the government agency in charge of both regulating and promoting the nuclear power industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate regulatory oversight from promotional responsibilities to remove conflicts of interest and ensure independent, stringent safety enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not forgo safety measures due to fear of litigation or protests
rubrics_metrics.description: TEPCO admitted that it had failed to take necessary measures for fear of inviting lawsuits or protests against its nuclear plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operators should prioritize safety upgrades and hazard mitigation even when such actions might provoke public opposition or legal challenges; transparency and stakeholder engagement are preferable to suppression of safety measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer passive venting systems over manually activated venting
rubrics_metrics.description: American nuclear scientists identified manually activated venting systems to be riskier than a passive approach five years prior to the accident. By 2011, new reactor designs used passive venting systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design venting systems that operate passively or automatically under accident conditions rather than relying on manual activation which may be delayed or impossible during extreme events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act on prior warnings and mitigate identified loss-of-power risks
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission warned of a risk of losing emergency power in 1991 and the Nuclear and Industrial Safety Agency referred to that report in 2004, but took no action to mitigate the risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators and operators must respond to identified vulnerabilities (e.g., risk of losing emergency power) with concrete mitigation measures in a timely manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conservative tsunami and flooding hazard assessments in design
rubrics_metrics.description: In-house TEPCO reports and government studies between 2000–2009 estimated potential tsunamis up to ~15 meters, but earlier TEPCO forecasts were much lower and protections were not implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt conservative, evidence-based tsunami and coastal flooding hazard estimates when designing and siting safety-critical equipment; revise assumptions as new scientific evidence emerges and protect critical systems accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect emergency diesel generators from flooding
rubrics_metrics.description: One of unit 1's EDGs failed as a result of a condensate coolant leak and earlier flooding; engineers reported the possibility that a tsunami could damage the generators and later doors were installed to prevent water ingress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure emergency diesel generators and their rooms are protected against water ingress, piping breaches, and other flood pathways (physical barriers, sealed penetrations, elevated siting where feasible).
